sections.h2: Can a Tennessee owner sign a transfer on death deed?
sections.html:
The General Assembly has been asked to authorize one. Senate Bill 984 of the 114th General Assembly proposed a "Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act," and House Bill 1793 and Senate Bill 2029 carried a revised version into the 2026 session. Before you sign anything, ask the register of deeds in your county, or a Tennessee attorney, whether a transfer on death deed is recordable today.

The bills matter even if you are still waiting, because they show what the Legislature has put in front of owners: a deed that passes a house to a named beneficiary at death, takes effect only if recorded before death, and leaves the owner free to sell or borrow in the meantime. This page walks through that text, then covers the recording rules that already govern any deed filed with a Tennessee register.

sections.h2: What would the proposed Tennessee transfer on death deed have to contain?
sections.html:
Senate Bill 984 sets three requirements, and the 2026 bills repeat them. The deed must contain the essential elements and formalities of an ordinary recordable deed, must state that the transfer to the designated beneficiary occurs at the owner's death, and must be recorded before the owner's death with the register of deeds in the county where the property sits.

  • Capacity: the same as the capacity needed to make a will.
  • Notice, delivery, acceptance and consideration: none of them is needed for the deed to work.
  • Warranty: the deed passes the property without covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed says otherwise.
  • Form: the bill includes a sample "Revocable Transfer on Death Deed" with names, mailing addresses, marital status, legal description, primary and alternate beneficiary, signature and notary acknowledgment.

Senate Bill 984 also adds transfer on death deeds to the list of recordable instruments in Tenn. Code Ann. 66-24-101(a)(12), so the register could take them with other deeds.

sections.h2: How could an owner revoke the deed, and what happens while the owner is alive?
sections.html:
Revocation must be written and recorded. Under Senate Bill 984, an instrument revokes a recorded transfer on death deed only if it is acknowledged by the owner after the deed it revokes and recorded before death in the same county. Qualifying instruments are a new transfer on death deed that revokes the old one expressly or by inconsistency, a revocation instrument, or an ordinary deed that expressly revokes it. A recorded deed cannot be revoked by writing across it or tearing it, and the sample form says it cannot be revoked by will.

During the owner's life the deed changes very little. The bill says it does not affect the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property, does not bind a buyer or lender who knows about it, does not affect creditors, and gives the beneficiary no legal or equitable interest. Nor does it affect eligibility for public assistance unless federal law requires otherwise. If the owner is one of several joint owners, a deed signed by joint owners is revoked only if all living joint owners revoke it.

The sample form adds practical advice in plain language. It says to record in each county where any part of the land lies, that an unrecorded deed can simply be destroyed, that the owner should not complete the form under pressure, and that telling the beneficiaries is recommended because secrecy can invite fraud.

sections.h2: What happens to the house, the mortgage and creditors at death?
sections.html:
The beneficiary takes the property subject to everything attached to it at the owner's death: mortgages, liens, contracts, and any claims of the bureau of TennCare for medical assistance. The interest depends on the beneficiary surviving the owner; if the beneficiary dies first the interest lapses, and shares among several beneficiaries pass to the others in proportion.

Creditors have a path to the house as well. If the probate estate cannot cover allowed claims or a spouse's or child's statutory allowance, the estate or a creditor may enforce the liability against property that passed by the deed. Senate Bill 984 gives eighteen months from death to start that proceeding. The 2026 summary of Senate Bill 2029 shortens the window to twelve months and adds a rule for a beneficiary who sells the house before an action starts: the creditor can pursue the beneficiary up to the value conveyed.

For a family planning to sell an inherited house, this means a sale by the beneficiary would still have to clear the mortgage and any recorded liens first. The deed avoids a probate filing for the transfer, but it does not erase debts that follow the property.

sections.h2: What do recording fees look like for a deed in Davidson County?
sections.html:
Any deed, including a transfer on death deed if one becomes recordable, goes through the register's fee schedule set by Tenn. Code Ann. 8-21-1001. Davidson County's register charges $5 per page for warranty deeds, quitclaim deeds and similar documents, with a $10 minimum and a $2 data processing fee, and it requires the name and address of the preparer on nearly every document.

The state's transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 under the Department of Revenue's rate page. The Senate bill says a transfer on death deed works without consideration, so whether any transfer tax applies when the beneficiary later takes title is a question for the register or an attorney once the law is settled.

  • Probate fee in Davidson County: $1, collected only when state tax is paid.
  • Required on the face of most documents: the preparer's name and address.
  • Releases and charters are the exceptions to that preparer rule.

sections.h2: What can an owner do now if the goal is to pass a house without probate?
sections.html:
Ask a Tennessee attorney which tools the current law gives you, and bring the property description, the deed by which you took title, and the names of everyone you want to benefit. Tennessee's recording rules exempt some family and trust transfers from the transfer tax. The Shelby County Register lists transfers into a revocable living trust by its creator and deeds from a trustee to carry out a testamentary devise among the exemptions under 67-4-409(a)(1).

If your concern is a house that is already inherited and needs to be sold, the practical question is who holds title and whether a court has appointed anyone to act. A register of deeds cannot give legal advice, but the office can tell you how documents must be formatted and what they will accept.

faqs.q: Is a transfer on death deed legal in Tennessee?
faqs.a: The General Assembly has considered bills to authorize one, including Senate Bill 984 in 2025 and House Bill 1793 and Senate Bill 2029 in 2026. Ask the register of deeds or a Tennessee attorney whether a transfer on death deed can be recorded before relying on one.

faqs.q: Does the deed have to be recorded?
faqs.a: Yes. Under the bills, the deed must be recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the property is located before the owner dies, and it has no effect otherwise.

faqs.q: Can the owner still sell the house after signing?
faqs.a: The bill text says the deed does not affect the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property during life, and the beneficiary has no legal or equitable interest until death.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary get a house free of the mortgage?
faqs.a: No. The beneficiary takes the property subject to mortgages, liens and TennCare claims that exist at the owner's death, and creditors can reach it if the estate falls short.

faqs.q: How is a transfer on death deed revoked?
faqs.a: By a recorded, acknowledged instrument: a later transfer on death deed, a revocation form, or a deed that expressly revokes it. The bill does not allow revocation by marking the deed or by will.
